extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners (prosecutors and litigators), patent examiners, and IPO members working on software-related §101 issues
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and case-digest for evaluating whether claims (especially software-related) are patent-eligible under 35 U.S.C. §101 using the Alice/Mayo framework and the USPTO 2019 Subject Matter Eligibility Guidance. Includes mapping to Federal Circuit and PTAB decisions and USPTO example guidance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alice/Mayo two-step framework
rubrics_metrics.description: First determine whether the claims are directed to a judicial exception (laws of nature, natural phenomena, or abstract ideas). If so, ask whether the claim elements, individually and as an ordered combination, transform the nature of the claim into a patent-eligible application (search for an 'inventive concept').
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the foundational test applied by courts (Mayo -> Alice). The document repeatedly applies this two-step framework across Federal Circuit and PTAB cases, using Alice step 1 ('directed to' inquiry) and step 2 ('inventive concept') as primary gates.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO 2019 Guidance — Alice Step 2A Prong 1 (categorize abstract ideas)
rubrics_metrics.description: Abstract ideas should be identified and grouped as mathematical concepts, certain methods of organizing human activity, and mental processes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use the three-category grouping to classify the claimed judicial exception when performing Step 2A; the Guidance provides examination examples mapped to Federal Circuit/Supreme Court decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: USPTO 2019 Guidance — Alice Step 2A Prong 2 (practical application)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim that recites a judicial exception is not 'directed to' that exception if the exception is integrated into a practical application of the judicial exception.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the judicial exception is integrated into a practical application, the claim is not directed to the exception under Step 2A and need not proceed to Step 2B. If not integrated, proceed to Step 2B (inventive concept). The Guidance supplies examples; PTAB decisions often analyze whether limitations integrate the exception into a practical application.

rubrics_metrics.name: Alice Step 2B — inventive concept (significantly more)
rubrics_metrics.description: After finding a claim directed to a judicial exception under Step 2A, determine whether additional claim elements provide an 'inventive concept' that is significantly more than the judicial exception (consider elements individually and as an ordered combination).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Federal Circuit often resolves eligibility at Step 2B; look for technical improvements, unconventional arrangements, or elements not well-understood, routine, and conventional. Berkheimer held that whether elements are 'well-understood, routine and conventional' is a question of fact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Identify whether limitations are 'well-understood, routine and conventional'
rubrics_metrics.description: Under Step 2B, recitations that are well-understood, routine, and conventional to a skilled artisan do not supply an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Per Berkheimer v. HP, this is a factual inquiry—if there is a material fact dispute about whether elements are routine/conventional, eligibility may not be decided as a matter of law (summary judgment inappropriate). Examiners and courts often rely on specification language and precedent to assess conventionality.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practical application evidence — technical integration and improvements
rubrics_metrics.description: To show a practical application (Prong 2) or an inventive concept, claim elements should integrate the judicial exception into a technological solution — e.g., improve computer functionality, provide a technological solution to a technical problem, or produce a specific technological result.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PTAB and Federal Circuit look for specifics: how the technology is integrated, what technical problem is solved, and quantifiable or described technological benefits (improved efficiency, reduced storage, improved operating efficiency). Mere automation or generic computer implementation is insufficient.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid merely adding generic computer components
rubrics_metrics.description: Recitation of generic computer activity (server, web page, database, communications network) that only links the abstract idea to a computer environment is insufficient to render a claim a practical application or inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PTAB routinely rejects claims where server/web-page/database steps 'merely add generic computer activity to deliver web pages and store data.' Claims should describe how the computer components are configured or operate in a non-generic, technical way.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specificity in claims and specification supports eligibility
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims and specification should include concrete details about structures, integration, timing, or other technical features rather than high-level descriptions.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practice tips: include multiple specific features tied to the problems of the environment; describe how technology provides the improvement; tie recited advantages to technology rather than mere economic efficiencies. The PTAB reversed some rejections where claims contained limitations addressing problems in a specific hybrid trading environment (e.g., timer mechanism).

rubrics_metrics.name: Ordered combination analysis (individual elements vs. combination)
rubrics_metrics.description: Even if individual claim elements are routine or abstract, the ordered combination of elements may provide an inventive concept — but courts/PTAB will scrutinize whether the combination is merely conventional automation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not assume ordered combination alone saves eligibility; show that the combination yields a non-generic technical improvement or solves a technical problem in a way not previously known. The PTAB has found ordered combinations insufficient when they simply link abstract ideas to computer use without improving computer function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims that are directed to improvements in computer functionality are more likely eligible
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims that specify an improvement in how computers operate (particular manner of summarizing/presenting information, improved data structures, non-generic arrangement of components) can be considered non-abstract and eligible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Cases like Enfish and others are cited where claims were held directed to an improvement in computer functionality rather than an abstract idea; show specificity in claim language to capture that improvement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Economic practices and market activity claims are likely 'methods of organizing human activity'
rubrics_metrics.description: Claims reciting fundamental economic practices (trading derivatives, intermediated settlement, basic market operations) are typically grouped as methods of organizing human activity and thus treated as abstract ideas under the Guidance.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When claims recite economic practices, focus drafting on technological features that integrate the economic practice into a practical application (e.g., technical mechanisms addressing hybrid electronic/paper environments). PTAB noted that core trading operations are 'basic concepts' akin to intermediated settlement.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use specification to define claim terms and show technological character
rubrics_metrics.description: Examiner and PTAB analyses frequently rely on specification statements to interpret claim elements (e.g., 'workflow stages' characterized as human activity vs. technical identifiers).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Draft specification to describe technical meaning, structure, and integration of claimed elements. Specifications that describe implementation details and technological advantages help arguments for practical application and inventive concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Show concrete limiting mechanisms (e.g., timers, identifiers) that address specific problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Including concrete mechanisms (timers, identifiers, specific network components) that meaningfully limit conventional practice can help demonstrate integration into a practical application or provide an inventive concept.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PTAB found that delaying execution with a timer and allocating orders upon expiration solved a hybrid-exchange problem and supported eligibility; emphasize how such mechanisms change the operation/behavior of the system rather than merely describe conventional steps.

rubrics_metrics.name: Demonstrate technological advantages, not only economic efficiencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Advantages recited in the specification and claims should be tied to technological improvements (improving computer function, removing communication advantages, reducing storage redundancy), not merely to economic benefits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: PTAB and USPTO guidance emphasize that showing technological improvements supports practical application findings; statements of advantage should be tied to claim elements and implementation details.

rubrics_metrics.name: Map case facts to USPTO guideline examples for examiner/court comparisons
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the 'Mappings' approach to identify USPTO Guidance examples most closely corresponding to the software technology and to compare case holdings with Guidance Prong One/Two considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The document's Mappings sheet indexes cases by technology position (software stack) and legal issue; use it to find closest USPTO example and anticipate Examiner/Board treatment. Note: Federal Circuit is not bound by USPTO Guidance and may analyze differently.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be aware of divergence between USPTO Guidance and Federal Circuit approaches
rubrics_metrics.description: USPTO Guidance emphasizes Step 2A practical application analysis and may avoid extensive Step 2B inventive concept discussion; the Federal Circuit is more likely to proceed directly to inventive concept analysis under Step 2B.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drafting and briefing strategies should address both approaches: demonstrate practical application per USPTO examples and, separately, show inventive concept/technical improvements for Federal Circuit review.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural labeling and outcome mapping (Y / N / Y & N / N/A / Probably Not)
rubrics_metrics.description: When summarizing caselaw, label outcomes consistently: 'Y' (all claims eligible), 'N' (all claims ineligible), 'Y & N' (some claims eligible, some not), 'N/A' (abstract idea found but remanded for factual inquiry on inventive concept), 'Probably Not' (see case assessment).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use these labels to quickly index and filter cases in the mappings table; they are practice-oriented shorthand for case results when comparing to USPTO Guidance.
